avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP (post-spinal-surgery trigger, possible mechanical contribution)

differential.key_features: Anatomically restricted distribution and asymmetric pattern; symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia argues against pure mechanical injury.
Spinal MRI required; sensory level and sphincter dysfunction absent here; MRI excludes.
Post-op ICU course increases risk; pattern of CSF dissociation and demyelinating EMG argues for GBS.
Sphincter and saddle anaesthesia absent; not consistent.

key_clinical_evidence: Surgery is a recognised immune-trigger for GBS; mechanical injury alone is restricted in distribution and timing.
Imaging rules out structural / surgical complication; GBS is diagnosed by Brighton-level clinical and laboratory criteria.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Symmetric ascending paralysis with CSF dissociation and demyelinating EMG indicates GBS triggered by the surgical inflammatory milieu, not direct surgical injury.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on mechanical / surgical injury rather than autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy.

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden bilateral thigh pain on postoperative day 11 after L1-L5 laminectomy, followed by rapidly ascending lower extremity weakness and tingling, with absent reflexes.

past_medical_history: Lumbar spinal stenosis L1-L5 with L4/5 spondylolisthesis — underwent L1-L5 laminectomy with L4/5 posterolateral fusion 11 days ago

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. T. is a 78-year-old woman presenting on postoperative day 11 after an uncomplicated L1-L5 laminectomy with L4/5 posterolateral fusion performed for lumbar spinal stenosis and spondylolisthesis. She had been ambulating with a walker and was progressing appropriately until postoperative day 9, when she had a single episode of loose stool without systemic symptoms. On postoperative day 11, she experienced sudden severe bilateral thigh pain, followed over the next several hours by ascending weakness and worsening tingling in both lower extremities. By the time of evaluation, she cannot stand or walk. The weakness developed rapidly over 12 hours. She is afebrile and her surgical wound appears to be healing well. The immediate concern is a surgical complication — epidural hematoma, hardware displacement, or infection — all of which must be excluded emergently. The single loose stool episode occurred 2 days before the onset of the neurological symptoms.

neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 1.8 L (predicted 2.6 L — 69%). NIF: -30 cmH2O. Post-operative day 11. Single loose stool episode on postoperative day 9. Surgical wound healing well — no erythema, no fluctuance. No fever. Spinal hardware intact on imaging. A post-surgical complication (hematoma, infection, hardware failure) must be excluded.

neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent bilateral patellar and Achilles. Trace bilateral upper extremity reflexes.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral hyperesthesia of distal lower legs and feet — allodynia. Bilateral tingling.
